statement: A named executive owns AI security risk. AI risk is reported to leadership on a defined cadence.
Every AI system and agent has a named business owner accountable for its actions and outcomes.
A cross-functional AI governance group, including security, legal, privacy, risk, and the business, operates under a documented charter.
AI security metrics and key risk indicators are defined, tracked, and reported with AI risk.
ACTOR controls are independently assessed on a defined cadence by internal audit or a qualified third party.

An AI acceptable use policy classifies approved tools by data sensitivity and use case, publishes a sanctioned path for requesting new tools, and defines prohibited uses and data that must not be entered into AI systems.
Users do not connect AI agents to company systems with their own credentials unless the Delegate (DEL) controls are in place.
AI policy is reviewed at least annually and whenever a significant new AI capability is adopted.
AI-enabled security tools are inventoried and governed under ACTOR like any other agent.
Each AI use case is assigned a risk tier based on data sensitivity, level of autonomy, and impact of its actions.
Higher-risk use cases require a documented risk assessment and approval before deployment.
AI risk appetite and thresholds are defined. Exceptions are approved, documented, and time-limited.
Every AI system passes a pre-deployment review against applicable ACTOR controls before production use, scaled to its risk tier.
An obligations register tracks the AI laws, regulations, and sector guidance that apply to each use case.
AI vendors and AI features embedded in existing software are assessed before use, including data use, training on customer data, and retention.
Contracts address data ownership, training on customer data, incident notification, audit rights, and access to usage logs and telemetry.
AI vendors are reassessed periodically, and an exit plan covers provider shutdown, acquisition, or model deprecation.
AI vendors disclose the model providers and subprocessors behind their service and give notice before changing them.
People who use AI are trained on safe use, data handling, and recognizing manipulated or incorrect output.
Developers, administrators, and security staff receive role-based training on AI-specific threats and controls.
An inventory lists every AI system, model, and AI feature in use, with owner, purpose, data accessed, and risk tier.
The inventory records model versions, providers, and hosting location for each system.
Retired models are removed from service, and their weights and associated data are disposed of or archived under policy.
Every agent is registered as a non-human identity with owner, purpose, scopes, connected systems, autonomy level, and a named halt authority with a documented halt procedure.
The registry records each agent's tools, connectors, plugins, and scheduled tasks.

Unapproved AI services, browser extensions, and employee-built agents are continuously discovered through network, endpoint, or SaaS monitoring, showing which tools are in use, by whom, and what data reaches them.
OAuth grants and API keys issued to AI services are discovered and reviewed.
For each AI system, the organization documents what data it can read, where prompts and outputs are stored, and how long they are kept.
AI systems and agents have a bill of materials covering models, datasets, libraries, prompts, tools, and accessible data, maintained in a standard machine-readable format such as CycloneDX or SPDX.
Each agent operates under its own identity. Agents never use a human user's credentials, session cookies, or MFA tokens.
Agent credentials are short-lived and narrowly scoped. No static secrets in prompts, configuration files, or code.
Agents acting for a user use delegation, not impersonation, so downstream systems record both the agent and the user.
A delegated agent's effective permissions are the intersection of the user's rights and the agent's allowed scopes, never the union.
Agents authenticate to each other, and delegation chains between agents have a defined maximum depth.
Agents receive read-only access by default. Write access is granted per tool with a documented justification.
What an agent may do without approval is defined for each risk tier.
Agents cannot grant permissions to themselves or to other agents.
Before an agent automates a process, the process is documented and the steps that require a human in or on the loop are identified.
Every agent action is assigned a risk tier. High and critical actions require explicit human approval before they run.

Approvals for high and critical actions use phishing-resistant authentication, such as a FIDO2 hardware key, bound to the specific action being approved. Critical actions also require user verification (PIN or biometric), and keys that agents could reach require a touch for every use.
One approval authorizes one action. An approval never grants session-wide elevation.
AI-assisted decisions that materially affect people can be reviewed by a human, and the basis for each decision is recorded.
Agent access is reviewed on the same cadence as privileged accounts, with the owner attesting to each scope.
Agent identities, tokens, connectors, and scheduled tasks are removed when the purpose ends or the owner leaves.
Each approved AI platform has a documented secure configuration baseline covering data retention, training opt-out, sharing, connectors, and admin controls.
Enterprise identity (SSO, and SCIM where supported) is used for AI platforms.
Configuration is checked against the baseline on a defined cadence and after vendor feature releases.
Self-hosted model endpoints and AI APIs require authentication and are not exposed beyond the users and systems that need them.
Plugins, extensions, connectors, and MCP servers are reviewed for requested permissions and source before installation.
Models and datasets come from approved sources and are verified before use.
Model files and AI dependencies are scanned for malicious code and integrity-checked with hashes or signatures.
Sensitive data is classified, and AI access to it is restricted by classification.
Retrieval sources used by AI enforce the same access controls as the systems they come from.
A privacy impact assessment is completed for AI use cases that process personal data.
Prompt and output retention is minimized, and deletion requests are honored across retrieval stores and fine-tuning data.

Before AI tools that search or summarize company data are enabled, existing permissions on files, sites, and mailboxes are reviewed and overshared access is remediated, because AI exposes whatever users can already reach.
Technical controls warn on or block sensitive data sent to unapproved AI tools, enforcing the acceptable use policy where training and culture do not reach.
Model, dataset, and agent providers supply provenance documentation, such as model cards, data sheets, attestations, or an AI bill of materials, before procurement.
Every dataset used to train, fine-tune, or evaluate a model has a recorded source, owner, usage rights, and collection date.
New data passes an intake gate before use, with checks for poisoned or anomalous samples, hidden triggers, sensitive data, and prohibited content.
Data from public or untrusted sources is quarantined and reviewed before it enters a training or fine-tuning pipeline.
Data lineage is tracked from source through each transformation to the model version it produced.
Datasets are versioned and integrity-protected with hashes or signatures, so the exact data behind any model version can be reproduced.
Model weights and fine-tuned models are access-controlled and encrypted at rest.
System prompts and agent instructions are version-controlled and changed through review.
Internally built AI systems follow a secure development lifecycle that includes threat modeling for AI-specific threats.
AI systems are adversarially tested before production release.
AI-generated code goes through the same review, testing, and scanning as code written by people.
System prompts are written on the assumption they will be disclosed. They contain no secrets and no security logic that depends on secrecy.
An agent that reads untrusted content does not hold high-impact write tools in the same session unless human approval gates those tools.
Untrusted content (web pages, email, documents, tool output) is treated as data and separated from instructions where the architecture allows.
Inputs are screened for prompt injection before reaching models that handle sensitive data or hold tools.
Downstream systems treat model output as untrusted and validate it before executing, rendering, or storing it.
Outputs are screened for sensitive data before leaving the trust boundary.
Customer-facing AI output is filtered for harmful, prohibited, or off-policy content.
Agent network egress is restricted to approved destinations.
Rate and spending limits cap runaway or abusive consumption.
Tool calls pass through a policy enforcement point that checks each action against the agent's scope and risk tier.
Query patterns that indicate model extraction or inversion attacks are detected and throttled.
Code that an agent writes or runs executes in an isolated sandbox.
Every agent can be halted immediately, and step or loop limits stop runaway agents automatically.
Retrieval sources accept content only from authorized contributors.
Changes to training data, fine-tuning data, and retrieval sources are logged and attributable.
Model behavior is re-evaluated after any training or data update before it returns to production.
Content ingested into retrieval stores is tagged with its source and trust level, so models and downstream controls can tell trusted content from untrusted content.
Agent long-term memory is scoped to a user or task, reviewable by its owner, and cannot be written from untrusted content without validation.
User feedback, ratings, and conversation data are reviewed for manipulation before they are used to retrain or tune a model.

Agent actions, tool calls, approvals, and the acting identity are logged with trace IDs that link the authorizing human to the agent and each step and tool call, with retention aligned to incident response needs.
Prompts and outputs are logged for systems in scope, and those logs are protected like the data they contain.
AI logs feed the central SIEM and are correlated with target-system logs to separate agent actions from human ones.
Alerts fire on indicators of manipulation: unexpected resources, scope creep, and unprompted requests for sensitive data.
Each agent has a behavior baseline covering systems accessed, volume, timing, and tools. Deviations generate alerts.
AI security alerts are routed to the security operations function with defined triage and escalation procedures.
Provider model version changes are tracked and treated as change events that trigger review.
Production models are evaluated against a defined test set on a regular cadence and after model updates.
Thresholds for accuracy, safety, and output quality are defined. A breach triggers review or rollback.
Vulnerabilities in AI frameworks, models, and libraries are tracked and remediated on defined timelines.
AI threat intelligence, such as MITRE ATLAS techniques, is reviewed and used to update controls.
Users have a simple way to report suspicious or unexpected AI behavior.
AI systems are red-teamed for prompt injection, data leakage, and excessive agency on a defined cadence.
The incident response plan defines AI incidents, including manipulation, data leakage, harmful agent actions, and model compromise.
Runbooks exist to disable any agent identity, connector, or scheduled task without affecting its owner.
AI incident scenarios, including halting a misbehaving agent, are exercised in tabletops at least annually.
Investigators can reconstruct an AI incident from prompts, context, tool calls, and approvals.
Evidence collection covers AI artifacts, including model versions, system prompts, and retrieval sources.
Containment options include revoking agent tokens, disabling tools, pausing scheduled tasks, and blocking AI services.
Models, prompts, and retrieval sources can be rolled back to a known-good version.
Poisoned data is identified and removed, and its downstream effects are assessed.
Critical processes that depend on AI have documented fallback procedures for when the AI or its provider is unavailable.
Fallback procedures are tested, including a provider outage and a forced model change.
AI incidents are reported to vendors, customers, and regulators as contracts and law require.
Lessons learned update controls, baselines, risk tiers, and evaluation test sets.
